analogy.p: A pathogen is like fire: it needs fuel (susceptible hosts) and a way to jump between trees (contact, water, air). Fire breaks are like isolation and vaccination: they remove the fuel or the path, so the fire cannot spread. Sprinklers and putting out hot spots are like hygiene and treatment. The analogy breaks down because pathogens can also hide in vectors and reservoirs, and unlike fire they reproduce and evolve (for example, becoming resistant to antibiotics).
analogy.t: A fire spreading through a forest

bullets: **Communicable disease** = a disease caused by a pathogen that can be passed from one organism to another.
Four types of pathogen: **bacteria, viruses, fungi, protists**. Bacteria and viruses are the two the specification highlights for spread in animals and plants.
Three routes to learn: **direct contact, water, air**. The specification also names **vectors** (e.g. mosquitoes for malaria) and contaminated **food** (salmonella).
Seven named diseases: measles, HIV, TMV (plants), salmonella, gonorrhoea, rose black spot (plants), malaria.
Prevention methods: **hygiene, destroying vectors, isolation, vaccination**, plus barrier methods (condoms), safe food handling and fungicides for plants.
Mark schemes reward the pattern: **named action + what it stops** (e.g. 'wash hands to remove bacteria from skin').
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA 4.3.1 asks you to understand that **pathogens** are microorganisms that cause infectious (communicable) disease, and that they spread **by direct contact, by water or by air**. You must then be able to **describe** how the spread of a named disease can be reduced or prevented. The key skill is matching the control measure to the route: a measure only works if it breaks the way that particular pathogen travels. Questions are usually set on the named examples in the specification, but they may also give you an unfamiliar disease and ask you to apply the three routes.

bullets: **Bacteria**: single-celled living organisms that can reproduce quickly inside the body. They make **toxins** that damage tissues and make you ill.
**Viruses**: much smaller than bacteria; they live and reproduce **inside host cells** and damage them as they burst out.
**Fungi**: some fungi (e.g. rose black spot) grow on plants and release **spores** that spread through wind and water.
**Protists**: single-celled eukaryotes; some are parasites that live in or on a host and often need a **vector** to move between hosts (malaria).
**Infectious dose**: more pathogens passed on means a higher chance of infection, which is why even small reductions in spread matter.
Link: the spread of disease can be modelled as a **chain**: source of pathogens, route of transmission, new susceptible host. Cutting any link stops the chain.
core.p: A pathogen is a microorganism that causes disease. Once inside a host it **reproduces rapidly**, so an infected organism contains vast numbers of pathogens, and some of these must leave the body and reach a new host for the disease to spread. Pathogens leave in body fluids (blood, mucus, saliva, droplets), in faeces and vomit, in infected plant tissue or on contaminated surfaces, so the way a pathogen is released tells you how it is likely to spread. Understanding this makes the prevention methods logical rather than a list to memorise.

bullets: **HIV** is spread by **sexual contact** or by **exchange of body fluids such as blood**, which can occur when drug users **share needles**.
**Gonorrhoea** is spread by **sexual contact**.
**Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV)** spreads by contact between diseased and healthy plants (leaves rubbing) and on contaminated hands and tools.
**Prevention**: use **barrier methods (condoms)**, do not share needles, screen donated blood, wash hands, and keep infected plants away from healthy ones.
**Why condoms work**: they form a physical barrier so body fluids carrying the pathogen cannot pass from one person to the other.
Direct contact diseases are often controlled by **changing behaviour** and by tracing and treating contacts, as well as by drugs.
core.p: Direct contact means the pathogen passes straight from an infected organism to a new host through touching, sexual contact or exchange of body fluids such as blood. No intermediate (like air or water) is needed, so the pathogen often has to survive only briefly outside the body. This route matters for sexually transmitted infections and for blood-borne infections, and in plants it happens when a healthy leaf touches an infected one. Preventing it means **stopping the contact or putting a barrier between hosts**.

bullets: **Salmonella** (bacteria) is spread by **eating food contaminated with the bacteria**, e.g. raw or undercooked poultry and eggs, or food prepared with unwashed hands or contaminated surfaces.
**Rose black spot** (fungus) is spread by **water** (rain splash) as well as wind, carrying spores to healthy plants.
**Prevention**: treat water (filtering and chlorination) and separate sewage from drinking water; boil water where its safety is not known.
**Food hygiene**: wash hands, keep raw and cooked food apart, store food at the right temperature and **cook thoroughly** to kill bacteria.
For plants: avoid overhead watering that splashes spores, and water at the base.
Link to health: a country's water supply and sewage treatment strongly affect how fast diseases spread, so this is also a development and population topic.
core.p: Some pathogens are spread when people **drink or use contaminated water**, or eat food that has been contaminated by water or by dirty hands. The bacteria or protists are present in the water, usually because sewage or animal waste has got into it, and they infect the gut or other organs after they are swallowed. In plants, water can also spread pathogens: splashing rain or irrigation carries fungal spores from leaf to leaf. Good water treatment and food hygiene are therefore among the most effective public health measures in the world.

bullets: **Measles** (virus) is spread by **inhalation of droplets** from the coughs and sneezes of an infected person.
**Rose black spot** spores are carried by **wind**.
**Prevention**: cover your mouth and nose with a tissue when coughing or sneezing, bin the tissue, wash hands, avoid crowded places when ill.
**Isolation**: keep infected people away from others (e.g. isolation rooms in hospitals) so droplets cannot reach susceptible people.
**Vaccination**: makes people immune so they cannot become infected and pass the pathogen on (the most effective control for measles).
Good ventilation reduces the concentration of droplets in a room.
core.p: Many pathogens are carried in the air in **tiny droplets** that are coughed, sneezed or breathed out by an infected person. Other people then **breathe in** the droplets, and the pathogen enters their respiratory system. Because you cannot see or avoid air, this route spreads infections very quickly in crowded places such as schools, buses and hospitals. In plants, **wind** carries fungal spores over long distances. Prevention aims to stop droplets being released, stop people inhaling them or make people immune.

bullets: **Malaria** is caused by a **protist**; the **mosquito** is the **vector** that picks it up from the blood of an infected person and passes it on when it bites a healthy person.
**Stop the vector breeding**: drain or cover standing water where mosquitoes lay eggs, and use insecticides.
**Avoid being bitten**: sleep under **mosquito nets** (often treated with insecticide), use insect repellent, cover skin.
**Reduce the reservoir**: treating infected people with anti-malarial drugs means fewer protists in the blood for mosquitoes to pick up.
Plants also have vectors: insects such as aphids carry some plant viruses between plants.
**Exam link**: if a question says 'a mosquito carries the disease' your answer must talk about **breeding** or **bites**, not coughs or hygiene.
core.p: A **vector** is an organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another without usually being harmed by it itself. The best example in your course is the **mosquito**, which spreads the protist that causes malaria. Vectors spread disease indirectly, so the best control is often to **target the vector** rather than the pathogen. This is why strategies such as removing breeding sites and using nets are so effective in tropical countries.

bullets: **Measles**: fever and a **red skin rash**. Spread by droplets in the air. Can cause serious complications such as pneumonia, brain damage or death. Prevented by **vaccination** (MMR) of young children.

**HIV**: initial **flu-like symptoms**, then the virus attacks the **immune cells**. If untreated the immune system is so badly damaged that the person cannot fight other infections or cancers (**AIDS**). Spread by sexual contact or exchange of body fluids (sharing needles). Controlled with **antiretroviral drugs**, which stop the virus replicating, and spread is reduced by condoms.

**TMV**: a plant virus. Gives a **mosaic pattern of discolouration** on leaves. The discoloured parts cannot carry out **photosynthesis**, so the plant grows poorly. Spread by contact; controlled by removing infected plants and keeping hands and tools clean.
Antibiotics do **not** work on viruses because viruses live inside host cells; this is a very common exam point.
**Why vaccination suits measles**: the virus spreads by air so it is hard to avoid, but a vaccine gives long-term immunity.
Exam hint: for HIV, always include **two** routes: sexual contact and blood or needle sharing.
core.h: Viral diseases: measles, HIV and TMV
core.p: Viruses reproduce inside host cells, so they cannot be killed by antibiotics, which is why prevention matters even more for them. Each of the three viral diseases in your specification has a different route and a different symptom pattern. You should be able to give a symptom as well as the route of spread because questions often ask for both.

bullets: **Salmonella** food poisoning: symptoms are **fever, abdominal cramps, vomiting and diarrhoea**, caused by the bacteria and the toxins they make. Spread via contaminated food (poultry, eggs).
**Control of salmonella**: poultry in the UK are **vaccinated** against Salmonella, and food is cooked thoroughly, with good hygiene during preparation.
**Gonorrhoea**: a sexually transmitted disease with **thick yellow or green discharge** from the vagina or penis and **pain on urinating**.
Gonorrhoea was once easily treated with **penicillin**, but many strains are now **resistant** to it.
**Reducing spread of gonorrhoea**: use **barrier methods such as condoms**, limit the number of partners, and treat infected people so they cannot pass it on.
Link: resistant strains show **natural selection** in action (see evolution and antibiotics).
core.p: Bacteria multiply by dividing, and they cause harm by damaging tissues and releasing toxins. Salmonella is spread by food, and gonorrhoea by sexual contact, so their controls are completely different even though both are bacterial. Treatment with antibiotics is possible but is complicated by **antibiotic resistance**, which makes prevention even more important.

bullets: **Rose black spot**: a fungal disease; **purple or black spots** appear on leaves, which turn yellow and drop early. Less leaf area means less **photosynthesis**, so the plant grows less.

Rose black spot **spread** by **water and wind** carrying spores. **Control**: use **fungicides**, and **strip and destroy** affected leaves so spores cannot spread (burning or bagging, not composting).
**Malaria**: caused by a **protist**; the person has **recurrent episodes of fever** and it can be fatal.
Malaria is spread by the **mosquito** (a vector); the protist spends part of its life cycle in the mosquito.
**Malaria prevention**: stop mosquitoes breeding, use mosquito nets, and treat cases with drugs.
These two show that a **fungicide kills fungi** while **insecticides** target the vector; always match the chemical to the organism.
core.h: Fungal and protist diseases: rose black spot and malaria
core.p: These two diseases show how different the control methods can be. Rose black spot is a plant fungus that stops leaves photosynthesising, while malaria is a protist disease of humans spread by a vector. In each case the cure is not the key point of the question: the key marks are for stopping the spread.

bullets: **Hygiene**: washing hands, cleaning surfaces and cooking food properly removes or kills pathogens before they reach a host.
**Destroying vectors**: insecticides, removing breeding sites or using nets reduces transmission by carriers.
**Isolating infected individuals**: stops them passing on the pathogen through contact or droplets.
**Vaccination**: stimulates the immune system so a person is protected; also protects others by **herd immunity**.
**Barrier methods**: condoms prevent exchange of body fluids.
**Treatment**: antibiotics (bacteria only), antiretrovirals (HIV), fungicides (plants) reduce the number of pathogens available to spread.
**Quarantine** and controls on moving plants or animals prevent diseases being carried to new areas.
core.h: Reducing and preventing spread: the general toolkit
core.p: All prevention methods work by breaking one link in the chain of infection: removing the source of pathogens, blocking the route, or protecting the host. You need to be able to name the method and say how it works. In hospitals, several methods are combined, for example hand-washing, isolation and cleaning, because no single method is perfect.

bullets: On a **graph of cases against time**, read values carefully and use the **scale**, quoting numbers from the axes with units.
**Percentage change** = (change ÷ original value) × 100. Always divide by the **original (starting)** value.
A steep fall after Year 0 suggests the programme is working; a levelling-off means few susceptible people remain.
**Correlation does not prove cause**: other changes (better hygiene, better treatment) could also lower cases, so say 'the data suggests'.
Vaccination does not help people who are already infected; it works **before** infection.
Not everyone can be vaccinated (e.g. very young babies or people with weak immune systems), so herd immunity protects them.
core.p: If a large proportion of a population is vaccinated, the pathogen finds it hard to move from one person to another, so even unvaccinated people are protected. This is called **herd immunity**. Graphs of cases against time before and after a vaccination programme are often used in exams. Because the cases fall as more people become immune, the pathogen has fewer susceptible hosts to infect.

bullets: **Hospital**: hand-washing with alcohol gel between patients, **isolating** infected patients, cleaning equipment, wearing gloves and masks, limiting visitors.
**School**: encourage vaccination, tell ill children to stay home, cover coughs, provide soap and tissues.
**Farm**: vaccinate livestock (e.g. poultry against salmonella), control vectors, quarantine new animals.
**Garden or farm crops**: remove and destroy infected plants and leaves, use fungicides, space plants, clean tools.
**Travel**: use mosquito nets, repellent and anti-malarial drugs in malaria areas; check vaccinations.
Always say what the action **prevents**, not just the action.
core.h: Applying your knowledge: hospitals and everyday life
core.p: Exam questions often set a context such as a hospital, a school or a farm and ask you to suggest how spread could be reduced. Here you apply the same three routes, but you need to give context-specific actions. Always link the action to the route: for example, hand-washing breaks the contact route, isolation rooms stop air-borne spread, and clean water prevents water-borne spread.

bullets: **Human defence systems**: skin, mucus and stomach acid are the body's own barriers that reduce infection after exposure.
**Vaccination**: memory cells give a fast secondary response, protecting individuals and populations.
**Antibiotics**: kill bacteria but not viruses; overuse leads to resistance.
**Plant disease**: nutrient deficiencies and pests also reduce growth, but pathogens are different because they are infectious.
**Photosynthesis**: TMV and rose black spot reduce leaf area able to photosynthesise, so plant growth falls.
**Ecology**: invasive pathogens and vectors can move with climate change and trade.
core.p: This spec point connects to many other parts of the course, and joined-up answers earn extra marks in 6-mark questions. The most common links are with the immune system (how the body deals with pathogens that do enter), with vaccination (how immunity is created), and with antibiotics and evolution (why resistant bacteria are a growing problem).

exam: **Command words**: 'Describe' = say what happens (route and prevention); 'Explain' = give a reason using because; 'Suggest' = apply knowledge to a new context.
**1 mark**: name a route (air, water, direct contact) or one prevention method.
**2 marks**: a method plus why it works, e.g. 'Wash hands (1) to remove bacteria from skin so they cannot spread by contact (1)'.
**3 marks**: describe how a named disease is spread and give one prevention; give the symptom if asked.
**4 marks**: two methods each with a reason, or route plus prevention for two diseases.
**6 marks**: structure it: route of spread, then prevention for each route, then a linked idea such as vaccination or herd immunity. Use a clear order and named examples.
Always **match the control to the route**: vector disease means vector control, air means isolation or vaccination, contact means barriers.
Graph questions: quote **two data points with units**, calculate percentage change using the original value, and use cautious wording such as 'suggests'.
If asked for a **symptom**, give the specific one (red rash, fever, mosaic leaves, black spots) not just 'ill'.

mistakes.r: Vaccination prevents infection by making a person immune; it does not cure existing disease.
Antibiotics only kill bacteria; they do not work on viruses.
mistakes.w: Antibiotics will treat measles or HIV.

mistakes.r: Malaria is spread by the mosquito vector, so control means stopping mosquitoes breeding and avoiding bites (nets).
Name the action (washing hands) and what it removes or prevents (bacteria on the skin).
mistakes.w: Just saying hygiene or clean it.

mistakes.r: Viruses reproduce only inside host cells; they are not cells.
mistakes.w: Viruses are living cells that divide.

mistakes.r: The mosquito is a vector that transfers the protist in its bite.
mistakes.w: Mosquitoes spread malaria by coughing or in the air.

mistakes.r: It is a fungal disease; fungicides treat it and infected leaves are destroyed.
Barrier methods reduce the spread of sexually transmitted infections by preventing contact with body fluids.
Divide the change by the original value, then multiply by 100.
mistakes.w: Percentage change divided by the new value.

summary: Know how pathogens (bacteria, viruses, fungi and protists) are spread by **direct contact, water and air**, how named diseases (measles, HIV, TMV, salmonella, gonorrhoea, rose black spot, malaria) are passed on, and how the spread of each can be **reduced or prevented**. This is a very common 4 to 6 mark theme because it asks you to link a disease to its route, then choose the control that breaks that exact route.

terms.d: A disease caused by a pathogen that can be passed from one organism to another.
Spread of a pathogen by touching, sexual contact or exchange of body fluids between an infected and a healthy organism.
Spread of pathogens in tiny droplets coughed, sneezed or breathed out and inhaled by another person.
An organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another, e.g. the mosquito in malaria.
Keeping infected individuals away from others to stop the pathogen spreading.
Introducing a harmless form of a pathogen into the body to stimulate white blood cells to make antibodies, giving immunity.
Protection of a population when enough people are immune so the pathogen cannot spread easily.
A method such as a condom that prevents pathogens passing between people during sexual contact.
Single-celled organisms that reproduce quickly and can make toxins; some cause disease.
A microorganism that reproduces inside host cells; antibiotics do not work against it.
A chemical that kills fungi, used to treat fungal plant diseases.
A single-celled eukaryotic organism; some are parasites, e.g. the cause of malaria.
A chemical that kills insects, used to control vectors such as mosquitoes.
A poison produced by bacteria that damages body cells and tissues.
When bacteria are no longer killed by an antibiotic because they have changed by mutation and been selected.

worked.ans: Malaria is spread by mosquitoes, which are vectors (1). Draining standing water and spraying insecticides stops mosquitoes breeding (1). Sleeping under mosquito nets stops them biting people (1) and so stops the protist being passed on (1).
worked.q: Malaria is a disease caused by a protist. Describe how its spread can be reduced. (4 marks)
steps: Stopping breeding: drain or cover standing water, use insecticides (1+1).
Avoid bites: sleep under mosquito nets, use repellent (1+1).
Treating infected people reduces protists that mosquitoes can pick up.

worked.ans: 65% decrease (2 marks). Checking: 0.65 x 2000 = 1300 and 2000 - 1300 = 700, so correct.
worked.q: The graph shows cases of a disease after a vaccination programme. Cases were 2000 in Year 0 and 700 in Year 4. Calculate the percentage decrease. (2 marks)

worked.ans: Measles is a viral disease spread through the air in droplets from coughs and sneezes, which others inhale (1). HIV is spread by direct contact, through sexual contact or exchange of body fluids such as blood when needles are shared (1). Spread of measles is reduced by vaccinating children so they are immune (1) and by isolating infected people so droplets do not reach others (1). Spread of HIV is reduced by using condoms as a barrier (1) and by not sharing needles (1). Both are caused by viruses so antibiotics do not work (bonus). Different routes need different controls.
worked.q: Compare how measles and HIV are spread and how the spread of each can be reduced. (6 marks)
steps: HIV: sexual contact or blood, condoms and not sharing needles.
Contrast the routes and link to blocking each one.
